samples.text:
Nowadays, many people spend most of their day sitting in front of a computer or watching TV, and they do not do much exercise. This lifestyle cause several problems, and in this essay I will discuss them and suggest how people can become more active.

The biggest problem is health. When people sit for many hours and do not move, they can easily put on weight, and this can lead to serious illnesses like heart disease and diabetes. Also, sitting too long is bad for the back and neck, especially for office workers who use computer all day. Another problem is mental health. Exercise helps people to feel relaxed and happy, so people who never do sport are more likely to feel stressed or depressed. Furthermore, when many people are ill, the country has to spend more money on hospitals, which is a problem for everyone.

There are some ways to encourage people to be more active. First, the government should build more parks, sports centres and cycle paths, and make them free or cheap, so everybody can use them. Second, companies can help their workers, for example by giving them a break every hour to walk around or by offering free gym membership. In addition, schools should have more PE lessons, because if children enjoy sport when they are young, they will continue it when they grow up. Finally, there should be advertisements on TV and social media to show people the benefit of exercise.

In conclusion, sitting too much can cause health problems for people and extra costs for the country. I think the government, companies and schools should all encourage people to do more physical activity and have more healthy lifestyle.
samples.why: Both parts answered with relevant problems and ideas · points listed with limited extension · formulaic linking (First, Second, Finally) · adequate vocabulary with some repetition · errors in agreement, articles and comparatives.

samples.text:
Modern lifestyles have become increasingly sedentary, with many people spending most of their working day at a desk and much of their free time in front of screens. This trend has serious consequences for individuals and society, although there are a number of ways to encourage people to move more.

The most significant problem is the impact on physical health. A lack of regular activity is closely linked to weight gain, which in turn raises the risk of conditions such as heart disease, type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure. Long periods of sitting can also cause back and joint pain, a common complaint among office workers. Physical inactivity affects mental wellbeing too, since exercise is known to reduce stress and improve mood, so people who rarely exercise may be more likely to experience anxiety or low energy. At a national level, these health problems place a heavy burden on healthcare systems, and they also reduce productivity when employees need time off due to illness.

Encouraging people to be more active requires making exercise easier and more appealing. Local authorities could invest in safe cycle lanes, well-maintained parks and affordable sports facilities, so that physical activity become part of everyday life rather than something requiring special effort. Employers also have a role to play, for instance by providing standing desks, encouraging walking meetings or subsidising gym membership. Schools are perhaps the most important place to start, because children who develop an enjoyment of sport are more likely to stay active as adults. Finally, public health campaigns could highlight that even small changes, such as taking the stairs or walking short distances, bring real benefits.

In conclusion, sedentary behaviour harms both physical and mental health and increases the pressure on public services. By making activity more accessible at home, at work and at school, governments and organisations can help people lead healthier lives.
samples.why: Clear position · problems for individuals and society extended with explanation · solutions organised by setting · good range of linking and topic vocabulary (sedentary, subsidising) · one agreement slip.

samples.text:
Over recent decades, daily life in many countries has become strikingly sedentary. Desk-based jobs, car-dependent commuting and screen-based leisure mean that many adults now spend the majority of their waking hours seated. This shift carries significant costs, but carefully designed interventions can make physical activity a more natural part of everyday routines.

The most serious consequences are for health. Prolonged inactivity is a major risk factor for obesity, cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes, and it contributes to musculoskeletal problems such as chronic back pain. The effects are not solely physical: regular movement is associated with better sleep, lower stress and improved mood, so its absence can leave people more vulnerable to anxiety and depression. These individual problems accumulate into a wider social burden. Health services must treat a growing number of preventable, long-term conditions, while employers face reduced productivity and higher rates of absence.

Simply urging people to exercise more has limited effect, because inactivity is largely a product of how environments and routines are structured. The most promising approach is therefore to design activity back into daily life. Towns that provide continuous cycle networks, pleasant walking routes and accessible green spaces make active travel the convenient choice rather than a sacrifice. Workplaces can contribute by offering flexible breaks, sit-stand desks and facilities such as showers and bicycle storage that make active commuting practical. Schools arguably have the greatest long-term influence, since a positive early experience of sport and play shapes habits for life; ensuring that physical education is varied and inclusive, rather than purely competitive, is key. Subsidised leisure centre membership can further lower barriers for low-income groups.

In conclusion, sedentary lifestyles damage physical and mental health and impose broader economic costs. Rather than relying on exhortation, societies should reshape their built environments, workplaces and schools so that being active becomes the easiest option.
samples.why: Both parts sufficiently addressed with extended, relevant support · argues why simple persuasion fails before offering solutions · skilful cohesion · wide, precise vocabulary (musculoskeletal, exhortation) · wide range of accurate structures.
